analysis.one_liner: Bans drug companies from paying generic makers to keep cheaper copies off the market.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to ban "pay-for-delay" drug settlements cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee with 12 cosponsors from both parties, but sat on the Senate calendar for over a year and never got a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban "pay-for-delay" deals, in which a brand-name drug maker pays a generic or biosimilar rival to keep its cheaper version off the market for years. It lets the Federal Trade Commission treat such deals as automatically anticompetitive and imposes civil penalties up to three times the value exchanged, while still allowing settlements that simply let the cheaper version launch early. It cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee with support from both parties but was never voted on by the full Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, employers, insurers, and taxpayers who buy prescription drugs — including federal programs, which the bill's findings note cover over 40% of the $325 billion spent annually on retail prescription drugs [S4]. Generic and biosimilar makers would also benefit by being able to sell sooner instead of collecting payments to stay out [S2][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers buying prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: Makes pay-for-delay settlements presumptively unlawful: if a brand company gives a generic or biosimilar filer anything of value and the filer agrees to stay off the market, the FTC can treat the deal as an automatic anticompetitive violation, with the companies bearing the burden of proving otherwise [S2][S3][S4].

Attaches real penalties: violators forfeit a civil penalty of up to three times the value of the deal, and a generic filer that participates loses its valuable 180-day first-filer exclusivity [S2][S4].

Targets the most expensive part of the market, biologics: the bill's findings note biological drugs represent more than 40% of all prescription drug spending and extend the ban to biosimilar-delay deals [S4].

Closes the paper trail: companies must certify under oath to the FTC and Justice Department that the agreements they filed are complete, including side deals and oral promises, so the payment terms cannot be hidden [S4].
Still allows legitimate settlements: deals that simply let the generic launch before patents expire, payments for reasonable litigation expenses, and covenants not to sue remain permitted [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug and biologic makers, which would lose the ability to pay rivals to delay competition and face civil penalties up to three times the value of a violating agreement [S4]. First-filing generic companies would also give up the option of collecting delay payments [S2].

drawbacks.text: Companies would have to prove a deal's procompetitive benefits by clear and convincing evidence, and the fact finder is barred from presuming that early-entry terms make a deal procompetitive [S4]. That high bar could push more patent disputes into full litigation instead of settlement — and litigation itself delays generic entry, sometimes for years.

Payments for litigation expenses are capped at $7.5 million in 2021, adjusted for inflation [S4]. In complex patent fights over expensive biologics, real litigation costs can exceed that, which could force cases to trial rather than settle.

The committee-reported version narrowed the bill: the original text applied to agreements entered into after June 17, 2013, but the substitute amendment applies only to agreements signed after enactment [S4] — meaning deals already struck before passage would be beyond its reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers and public payers is large and direct: generics run 80–85% below brand prices, and pay-for-delay deals exist precisely to postpone that discount [S4]. The main risks — chilled settlements and more litigation — are real but modest next to the monopoly extension the bill stops, and the bill already carves out the settlement types that raise no competition concern [S3][S4]. The bill's biggest design weakness is its own doing: dropping retroactivity spares every deal struck before passage. Overall a well-aimed consumer bill with manageable side effects.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee in December 2021 and sat on the Senate's calendar of pending business for over a year, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on April 28, 2021 with a bipartisan group of co-introducers led by Republican Chuck Grassley, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee [S1][S4][S6].
On July 29, 2021, the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment [S6].

On December 9, 2021, the committee formally reported the bill with the substitute amendment and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 180 [S3][S6]. The substitute dropped the original's retroactive coverage of agreements dating back to June 2013 [S4].
The bill then sat on the Senate calendar with no floor debate or vote for the remaining thirteen months of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2023 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug and biologic makers came out ahead: they kept the ability to settle patent disputes by paying generic and biosimilar rivals to stay off the market, preserving monopoly prices, while everyone buying drugs kept paying them.

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through introduction and committee markup

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Klobuchar, giving it bipartisan sponsorship

for.name: Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee with a substitute amendment on December 9, 2021, after the committee voted it favorably in July

for.name: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats and 5 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, bringing total sponsorship to 12 senators from both parties

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Left the bill on the Senate calendar without ever scheduling it for a floor vote

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split across party lines in both directions — 7 of 48 Senate Democrats and 5 of 50 Senate Republicans signed on, led by a Democrat (Klobuchar) and a Republican (Grassley) — but no floor vote ever tested where the full chambers stood.

industries.note: The bill ends their ability to pay generic and biosimilar rivals to postpone competition, extends the ban to biologics — over 40% of drug spending — and adds penalties up to three times a deal's value. Their gain from delay comes directly out of what patients and public programs pay for medicine.

First-filing generic companies lose the option of collecting payments to stay off the market and face penalties for participating, but they gain the right to sell sooner and keep their full 180-day exclusivity unless they join a violating deal. Their normal business — selling cheaper copies earlier — runs alongside consumers' interest.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employers who pay drug bills
industries.note: Earlier generic and biosimilar entry lowers the drug costs that insurers and self-insured employers absorb, alongside patients at the pharmacy counter.
